name: pixiewps
desc: Offline Wi-Fi Protected Setup brute-force utility
why: Offline WPS PIN recovery exploiting weak entropy in the protocol, a revealing look at how a Wi-Fi handshake can leak secrets.

brief.what_it_is: Pixiewps is a C command-line tool that brute-forces a Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) PIN offline, using the "pixie-dust" weakness in some implementations' low or non-existent entropy. The user feeds it values captured from a WPS exchange (public keys, hashes, authentication key, nonces) and it prints the PIN if the target is vulnerable. Since version 1.4 it can also recover the WPA-PSK from a complete passive capture (M1 through M7) on some devices, using --mode 3. The README says the tool is meant for educational purposes only.
brief.why_it_exists: The README contrasts it with online WPS brute-forcing in tools like Reaver or Bully, which can take hours; Pixiewps aims to get the PIN in seconds or minutes, if the target is vulnerable. It is based on Dominique Bongard's 2014 offline attack research and started as a community project on the Kali Linux forums.
brief.how_it_works: The offline attack works from values captured during a WPS exchange rather than by sending guesses to the access point. The README says the common usage needs a modified Reaver or Bully that prints the Authentication Session key (--authkey), and recommends reaver-wps-fork-t6x. The --dh-small (-S) option, which relies on private key 1 and public key 2, is documented as deprecated and should never be used with Reaver.

brief.install_notes: Needs build-essential to compile. Versions before 1.2 need libssl-dev. Versions 1.4 and later use multi-threading and need POSIX threads (libpthread). OpenSSL is optional, enabled with make OPENSSL=1 for speed. Install with sudo make install. Practical use also needs a modified Reaver or Bully that prints the authentication session key; the README recommends reaver-wps-fork-t6x. Windows builds are possible through MinGW with pthread support. Since 1.4.1 it has been in the OpenWrt and LEDE official repositories. The README also mentions a man page.
brief.standout: The attack needs no online guessing against the access point: it works from captured handshake values and can finish in seconds, not hours. Version 1.4 added recovery of WPA-PSK from a passive capture on some devices, which the README presents as a way to show how a WPS exchange can leak the network passphrase.
brief.status: Unknown from the README alone. The README has no release date, last-commit date, or maintenance note. It documents version numbering and mentions 1.4.1 and OpenWrt/LEDE inclusion, but I did not check the releases or commit pages, so I can't confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The README says it is meant for educational purposes only. Licensed GPL v3 or later. Build needs a C toolchain, and older versions need OpenSSL and newer ones need pthreads. Usable only with a modified Reaver or Bully to get the authkey. Recovering WPA-PSK works only on some devices, and only with --mode 3. The --dh-small option is deprecated and the README says it should never be used with Reaver. The README's git clone URL (wiire/pixiewps) differs from the homepage (wiire-a/pixiewps). The Windows section has a typo, 'phtread'.
quotes: It is meant for educational purposes only.

As opposed to the traditional online brute-force attack, implemented in tools like Reaver or Bully which aim to recover the pin in a few hours, this method can get the PIN in only a matter of **seconds** or **minutes**, depending on the target, **if vulnerable**.
Since version 1.4, it can also recover the **WPA-PSK** from a complete passive capture (M1 through M7) for some devices (currently **only some devices** which work with `--mode 3`).
